claims.text: The modeled alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The modeled alloy is a metastable single-phase beta-BCC material.
The new approach separately computes lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
Lattice thermal conductivity will be computed from ab initio phonon dispersions and force constants while accounting for lattice distortion.
Electronic thermal conductivity will be calculated using separate electron-scattering-rate estimates.
The new approach will outperform earlier Debye-based models.
Earlier comparison models use a single Debye temperature and do not separate lattice and electronic heat transport.
Intrinsic lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr enhance phonon scattering.
Interstitial oxygen acts as an additional phonon-scattering center.
For oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr above 300 K, lattice thermal conductivity will be approximately 30% below previous convolved or Debye-based estimates.
Above 300 K, the lattice thermal conductivity will exhibit an approximate inverse-temperature dependence.
The electronic thermal-conductivity contribution will remain nearly temperature-independent.
Electronic heat transport will remain relatively unaffected by lattice distortion and interstitial oxygen.
Adding approximately 1 wt.% oxygen will reduce the lattice thermal-conductivity component by about 20% below 200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions are comparable in HfNbTaTiZr.
The approach is limited to homogeneous, well-sintered samples with near-zero or approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to temperatures below 200 K or from 300 to 1200 K.
Microstructural defects and processing variations omitted from the model may affect the predicted conductivities.
The 3-omega method and Hall-effect measurements can independently quantify lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions over 100–1200 K.

contradictions.description: The initial state labels both oxygen-free and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen variants as defect-free, while the oxygen-containing variant is simultaneously described as containing interstitial oxygen scattering centers. Interstitial oxygen is a point-defect species, so the oxygen-bearing sample is not literally defect-free.
